title: Hodges and Sons: explaining financial accounting, the accounting equation and a client's income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement
participant_role: General accountant at Hodges and Sons briefing the senior partner before meeting a potential client
judge_role: Senior partner at Hodges and Sons who wants a briefing on how the accountant will explain financial accounting to the potential client
scenario:
You are to assume the role of a general accountant at HODGES AND SONS, one of the largest accounting firms in the country. The firm has an opportunity to contract a new client. The senior partner (judge) has asked you to meet with the potential client to establish the relationship and explain financial accounting principals. The senior partner (judge) has asked for a briefing of the meeting before you meet with the potential client.

The potential client is extremely worried about his finances. Unfortunately, his previous accounting firm stole thousands of dollars due to fraudulent accounting practices. The actions of the previous firm lead to the potential client filing for bankruptcy several years ago. The potential client has decided to take an active role in his finances and would like to understand the true concept of financial accounting; how various financial transactions effect the accounting equation. He has requested that you explain in detail the nature of his income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statements for 2015 which he has provided the firm. You will meet with the senior partner (judge) to present findings prior to meeting with the potential client.

The senior partner (judge) is expecting the following information:
- Explain the concept of financial accounting.
- Describe how financial transactions effect the accounting equation.
- Explain the nature of income statements using the client's actual income statement.
- Discuss the nature of balance sheets using the client's balance sheet.
- Explain the components of a cash flow statement and why the cash flow statement is so important to any business.

You will brief the senior partner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the senior partner's (judge's) office. The senior partner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your findings. After you have conducted the briefing and have answered the senior partner's (judge's) questions, the senior partner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer defines accounting as a system for identifying, recording and communicating financial information, walks through the accounting equation (A = L + OE) with examples of how transactions keep it balanced, and then explains each bolded section of the client's actual income statement (net income $502,126) and balance sheet (total assets $769,001, liabilities $17,020, equity $751,981). It closes with the three sections of the cash flow statement and why a negative net change in cash is a red flag.

answer: Accounting is a system of recording and summarizing business and financial transactions; it identifies, records and communicates relevant, reliable and comparable information to interested users
Business entity concept: the business is accounted for separately from its owner
Dual aspect concept: every transaction has two effects, which is why debits always equal credits
Going concern and accounting period concepts: the business is assumed to continue indefinitely, and its life is split into periods so statements can be prepared regularly
Cost and money measurement concepts: only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded, at cost
Matching concept: expenses of a period, paid or not, are matched against the revenue they helped earn

by_task.task: Effects of transactions on the accounting equation
answer: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity (shareholders' equity for a corporation)
A company can pay for an asset with another asset (cash), with a liability (debt) or with owner's equity (investment or retained earnings)
Liabilities can be paid down with assets such as cash or by taking on new debt
Every transaction keeps the equation in balance, and the balance sheet shows this: $769,001 = $17,020 + $751,981
Example: buying DJ equipment on account raises Equipment (asset) and Accounts Payable (liability) by the same amount

by_task.task: Nature of the income statement (client's 2015 statement)
answer: An income statement shows financial performance over a period of time, here the year ended December 31, 2015
Operating revenue $540,253 is money earned from selling the company's services; cost of services sold $23,420 is what it cost to provide them, leaving gross profit of $516,833
Operating expenses $13,163 combine selling expenses ($1,995) and administrative expenses ($11,168) that are not directly tied to producing the service
Income from operations $503,670 = gross profit minus operating expenses; other revenue of $500 is bank interest earned outside normal operations
Net income before tax $504,170, less federal income tax $2,044, gives the bottom line net income of $502,126; units of services sold (1,285) shows volume for the period

by_task.task: Nature of the balance sheet (client's 2015 statement)
answer: A balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and capital at a single point in time, December 31, 2015
Assets $769,001 are resources the company owns with future economic value: cash $502,126, accounts receivable $1,875 and DJ equipment $265,000
Liabilities $17,020 are debts owed to others: two accounts payable ($6,275 and $10,245) and a $500 note payable
Owner's equity $751,981 is the owner's investment minus withdrawals plus net income since the business began
Total assets equal total liabilities plus owner's equity, proving the accounting equation

by_task.task: Nature of the cash flow statement
answer: Shows a company's gross cash receipts and gross cash payments for a period and tells a lot about liquidity
Operating activities: cash from day-to-day business
Investing activities: cash spent on capital expenditures and acquisitions
Financing activities: cash from borrowing or selling stock and cash used to repay loans or pay dividends

Each section nets cash in and cash out; the net increase in cash should be positive. A negative net change is a red flag that the company may not have enough cash to meet obligations and must be monitored closely

calculations.label: Income statement flow, 2015
steps: Net sales $540,253 minus cost of services sold $23,420 = gross profit $516,833
Selling expenses $1,995 + administrative expenses $11,168 = total operating expenses $13,163
Gross profit $516,833 minus operating expenses $13,163 = income from operations $503,670
Plus interest revenue $500 = net income before tax $504,170
Minus federal income tax $2,044 = net income after tax $502,126

judge_question_answers.question: Explain what the other revenue/expense section of an income statement is and give an example of another type other revenue (not interest income)?
answer: Other revenue and other expenses come from activities outside the company's core operations
Example: a shoe store renting out spare space earns rental income, or a soda machine in the store earns vending income
Related costs, such as maintenance on the soda machine, would be other expenses

judge_question_answers.question: How did you feel the potential client did in 2015 based on the income statement and balance sheet?
answer: Ryan the Rapper is a very healthy company based on the 2015 statements
The income statement shows revenue was more than enough to cover all expenses and leave a solid profit of $502,126
The balance sheet shows the company is very liquid ($502,126 cash against only $17,020 of liabilities) and is managing its assets well relative to its debts

tables.title: The accounting equation on the December 31, 2015 balance sheet

key_concepts.definition: An information and measurement system that identifies, records and communicates relevant, reliable and comparable information about a business to interested users.
Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. Every transaction affects at least two items and keeps the equation in balance.
The business's records are kept separately from the personal finances of its owner.
Expenses incurred in a period, whether paid or not, are recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped earn.
The assumption that a business will keep operating indefinitely, which affects how assets and liabilities are valued.
A financial statement that shows revenues, expenses and net income over a period of time. Gross profit = Net sales minus cost of sales; Income from operations = Gross profit minus operating expenses.
Operating revenue comes from the company's main day-to-day business; other revenue (interest, rent, vending) comes from activities outside core operations.
A financial statement that lists assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a specific point in time and proves the accounting equation.
The owner's investment in the business minus withdrawals plus net income since the business began; also total assets minus total liabilities.

A statement of cash receipts and payments for a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities. The net change in cash should be positive; a negative change is a red flag for liquidity.
How easily a company can pay its short-term obligations with cash or assets that quickly become cash.
